citeinfo.title: Digital elevation model (DEM) data for the Colorado River corridor in Grand Canyon National Park and Glen Canyon National Recreation Area (2021)
citeinfo.othercit: Additional information about Originators: Sankey, Joel B, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3150-4992; Bransky, Nathaniel, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3113-7491; Kohl, Keith, https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6812-0373; Gushue, Thomas M, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7172-2460; Bedford, Ashton F, https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6290-0897; Durning, Laura E, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3282-2458

descript.abstract: The 2021 Digital Elevation Model (DEM) dataset consists of single band rasters at 1-meter pixel resolution that were generated to orthorectify four band ortho imagery acquisition, and to support development of additional GIS products. Each pixel represents the elevation of the ground surface at that point expressed as NAD83(2011) ellipsoid height. A Digital Surface Model (DSM) was generated by automatic correlation of stereoscopic imagery collected from approximately 8,000 ft to 11,000 ft above mean sea level at 20-cm resolution with one Leica ADS100 digital push-broom multi-spectral sensor on each of two aircraft May 29, 2021 – June 4, 2021. The DEM was generated by removing the aboveground features from the DSM by filtering process. Data were collected during a period of low steady river flow of approximately 8,000 cubic feet per second released from Glen Canyon Dam. The data are for the segment of the Colorado River corridor from Glen Canyon Dam downstream to Pearce Ferry, AZ.
descript.purpose: The primary purpose of each of these digital topographic datasets was for the orthorectification of multispectral images acquired during a respective airborne data acquisition mission. These digital surface models (DSMs) and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) can be used for scientific research and production of GIS products such as topographic change detection, geomorphological analysis, and vegetation mapping. Sharing these digital data products can promote research at Grand Canyon and help provide free and easy access to federally produced scientific datasets.
descript.supplinf: These data represent continuous raster data. Data users should read the entire metadata record for each data product and acquire the cross reference manuscripts where applicable to have a complete understanding of how each data product was created. Users should not use these data for critical applications without a full awareness of their limitations. The data are specific to the uses identified and any other use of these data could be inappropriate. Users should be aware that topographic or other landscape changes may have occurred since the data were collected and that some areas of the data may no longer represent actual surface conditions. Accuracy assessments were performed to show the limitations of estimating elevation of locations on the landscape. However, accuracy assessments have limitations based on methods used to collect control points or features used to mark control points. The accuracy assessments are not relevant to water. Data are less accurate on water, steep slopes, and rough terrain. These data should not be used for navigational purposes, or any other uses related to travelling in the backcountry of Grand Canyon National Park. Any conclusions drawn from the analysis of this information are not the responsibility of the U.S. Geological Survey or its partners. Acknowledgement of the U.S. Geological Survey by referencing the data release citation would be appreciated for products derived from these data.

procstep.procdesc: Data acquisition: Multispectral digital imagery was acquired from May 29 through June 4, 2021 at altitudes of 8,000 ft to 11,000 ft (above mean sea level) using one Leica ADS100 digital multi-spectral sensor on each of two aircraft. For any given section of the river corridor, approximately five or six overlapping linear flightlines of image data were acquired. Color Infrared (CIR) and Natural Colors (RGB) ortho images at 20-cm pixel resolution were derived using photogrammetric ortho-rectification process. Panchromatic viewing angles were collected at 25.6° forward, at -19.4° backward, and near nadir at 2° forward. This provided the stereoscopic image data that was the basis for the processing of the DSM by automatic correlation. The digital surface model (DSM) product was generated to orthorectify the ortho imagery and to provide an accurate surface model for use in additional GIS products. The DSM is a reflective surface DSM which provides elevation data on open ground (e.g., such as bare soil, rocks, and water), as well as aboveground terrain features including buildings, trees, and vegetation that cover otherwise open ground. To generate the DEM, the aboveground features were removed from the DSM by filtering process. Thus, the DEM provides elevation data of the ground surface. The DEM data consists of 15 separate files, listed from Zone1 through Zone15.

Data Processing to create GCMRC DEM 2021 raster data: Step 1 – Step 1 – Overflight imagery was collected from May 29, 2021 – June 4, 2021 by contractor Fugro, Inc. United States Geological Survey staff manned a minimum of two GPS receivers that were within 50 km of the daily flight plan daily during overflights (stations referenced include NGS station point identifiers DG5953, DG5952, GP0592, GQ0305, AI5115, DN3649, FR0993, GR0381), and positioned 156 ground control panels to aid in aerotriangulation of the DSM dataset. Of the 159 panel locations, 112 were provided to be used in work completed by contractor Fugro, Inc., and 47 were retained by United States Geological Survey staff for use in data product evaluation.

Data Processing to create GCMRC DEM 2021 raster data: Step 2 – This step was completed by contractor Fugro, Inc. The digital surface model (DSM) was autocorrelated in XPRO and reviewed in Fugro’s proprietary software. The surface was reviewed for thoroughness and project area coverage. After noise removal, the DSM was mosaicked into USGS quarter quadrangle tiles with a 1-meter cell size. The DSM is a reflective surface DSM which provides elevation data on open ground (e.g., such as bare soil, rocks, and water), as well as aboveground terrain features including buildings, trees, and vegetation that cover otherwise open ground. To generate the DEM, the aboveground features were removed from the DSM by filtering process.

Data Processing to create GCMRC DEM 2021 raster data: Step 3 – DEM zones were created with identical spatial extents of earlier years of DSM data. The necessary tiles for each zone were identified in ArcGIS 10.8.1. Using ENVI 5.8.1 full extent tiles were mosaicked together using the seamless mosaic tool and exported to an ENVI .dat file type from the original .tif format. These mosaicked rasters were larger in spatial extent than necessary and were resized using the 2013 DSM zone extents for the same zone using the resize raster tool in ENVI. The areas outside of the river corridor had values of –999999 (no data), while all other zones/years have outside values of 0. To change outside values from the no data value to zero, a second seamless mosaic was applied using a binary dataset that replaced the no data values with a value of zero, while maintaining the true river corridor elevation values. These final zone files were exported as TIFF files during the second seamless mosaic process. The data consists of 15 separate files, listed from Zone1 through Zone15.

Data Quality Assessment and Quality Control (QAQC): Contractor Fugro, Inc. who acquired and processed the data stated the following about quality assurance for the delivered data. The ground control and airborne GPS data stream were validated through a fully analytical bundle aerotriangulation adjustment. The DEM data was checked against the project control. Topographic data was checked for edge match, consistency of attribution, and cartographic quality through visual inspection. A complete iteration of processing was performed to ensure that the acquired data was complete, uncorrupted, and that the entire project area had been covered without gaps between flight lines, voids, or missing data. Completed 2021.
An accuracy assessment of these data that compares DSM pixel elevation values to survey control point elevations has been completed by the USGS staff and is reported in tables in this data release. Completed 2023.

Finalize Data for Dissemination: Data sent to the Southwest Biological Science Center Data Steward for dissemination and preservation per USGS Data Management Policies SM 502.6, SM 502.7, SM 502.8 and SM 502.9 (1 October 2016).

enttyp.enttypd: This continuous raster dataset is a Digital Elevation Model of images collected from May 29, 2021 – June 4, 2021 and consists of 1-meter pixels. Each pixel represents the ground surface elevation at that point expressed as NAD83(2011) ellipsoid height. Pixel values of 0 indicate no elevation data. This dataset extends from Glen Canyon Dam, 15.8 river miles upstream of Lees Ferry to 282 river miles downstream from Lees Ferry. The data consist of 15 separate files, listed from Zone1 through Zone15.
